title: Speculations Concerning the First Ultraintelligent Machine
publisher: Advances in Computers, vol. 6, Academic Press
pitch: The source of the phrase 'intelligence explosion'. Good argues an ultraintelligent machine could design better machines, and would be the last invention we need, if it stays docile.
toc_note: Guide by theme. The paper's own section list was not checked against an official copy.

chapters.g: Good defines a machine that can far surpass any human in every intellectual activity.
Since designing machines is an intellectual activity, such a machine could design better ones, leading to an intelligence explosion.
Such a machine would be the last invention humans need make, provided it is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control.
Most of the paper speculates on how to build it, using ideas about meaning, memory and cell assemblies in the brain.

ideas: An ultraintelligent machine could improve itself.
That would cause an intelligence explosion.
Safety depends on the machine staying docile.

args.a: The first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention we need.
args.c: Later in life Good reportedly became more worried, and many now see the 'docile' condition as the whole problem.

quotes.text: Thus the first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control.
quotes.src: Speculations Concerning the First Ultraintelligent Machine, 1965, via Wikiquote

questions: Why is 'provided that the machine is docile' the most important part of the quote?

quiz.q: What phrase did Good make famous?
